transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-13
Start time (UTC): 16:30
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Clarke (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Lina Torres (BrightCart Eng Lead), Marcus Reed (BrightCart CTO), Tasha Kim (BrightCart PM)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough for BrightCart's chat/text gen use case. Focus on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and retry/backoff strategies. Discussed sandbox access, security concerns (SAML, KMS), and next steps to run a short PoC benchmark. Some transcription glitches present; names and acronyms occasionally mis-recognized.

Topics covered:
- BrightCart current stack and latency targets
- Demo of Redwood hosted chat endpoint (streaming)
- Parameter guidance and token budgeting
- Retry/backoff patterns and idempotency guidelines
- Security/compliance notes (SOC2, KMS, VPC options)
- Next steps and PoC planning

Action items (recap in call):
- Send sandbox keys + quickstart (Ethan)
- Bench script and runbook (Priya)
- Confirm VPN maintenance window for PoC (Lina)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. I'm Ethan with Redwood, AE. With me is Priya from our SE team. How are you doing, Lina, Marcus, Tasha?
[00:08] Lina: Doing good, thanks. Excited to see the hosted demo. We want to validate streaming for our customer chat flows.
[00:12] Marcus: Yup, we'll probably talk infra as well — we care about P95 latency under 400ms for short messages.
[00:18] Priya: Great, that's super helpful. We'll tailor the demo. Quick question — what are you running now for the model stack? In-house transformer endpoints or third-party API?
[00:27] Lina: Currently a mix. We have an internal endpoint backed by a custom quantized model, but it's flaky at scale. We also use an external provider for critical flows — cost's high though.
[00:36] Ethan: Makes sense. Today's walkthrough will show hosted API basics — streaming behavior, how to tune generation parameters and practical retry patterns. We'll also show Console glimpses for metrics and cost breakdown.
[00:46] Tasha: Sounds good. Also, security — we need SOC 2 evidence and KMS integration info.
[00:50] Ethan: Absolutely, we'll cover that and I'll send docs after.
[00:54] [01:05] Priya: Alright I'll share my screen for a quick live demo. Give me a sec.
[01:12] [01:20] Priya: Okay so this is the Redwood Console sandbox. We're hitting the hosted chat endpoint — examples use streaming. Notice on the right there's a tokens and cost preview for each call.
[01:31] Priya: I'll run a sample prompt, short user message, watch the stream come in.
[01:40] [01:45] Priya: (typing) "User: what's the fastest route from A to B?" 
[01:48] Speaker 2: ...and you can see each token chunk arrives as a partial event. If your client uses server-sent events or websocket you can pipe those to the UI — low latency, incremental render.
[01:58] Lina: Are those SSE events in order always? We saw reordering previously with our in-house stack.
[02:04] Priya: With hosted API the runtime guarantees chunk order per request; reordering only happens in rare network retries. We also include sequence metadata in events so your client can detect missing pieces.
[02:18] Marcus: What's your P50/P95 on streaming for small 20–40 token responses?
[02:23] Priya: On standard low-cost tier P50 is ~60–80ms for first byte in our benchmarks, P95 around 200–350ms depending on region and payload. For guaranteed low tail we recommend Dedicated pools.
[02:36] Tasha: How about cost predictability vs jitter from batching?
[02:40] Ethan: Good point — Console Optimize suggests batching parameters. There's an Optimize recommendation engine that suggests batch sizes and cache hints based on your workload. We can run an analysis on your historical logs.
[02:52] [03:10] Priya: Now parameterization — temperature, top_p, max_tokens. For deterministic summarization we set temperature to 0–0.2, top_p to 0.7–0.9; for creative chat higher temp like 0.8. Also use max_tokens to cap costs per response.
[03:26] Priya: Demo: change temperature from 0.2 to 0.8 and you'll see more varied continuations.
[03:33] Lina: Is there any server-side rate limiting we should be aware of? We have bursts from tens of thousands of small events.
[03:40] Ethan: Hosted has rate limits per API key and org quotas. For bursty traffic we recommend Dedicated or apply burst capacity. Also Console has per-token and per-route views so you can see hotspots.
[03:52] Marcus: We need to preserve exact message order in some flows; can you do idempotent retries?
[03:57] Priya: Yes — we support idempotency keys for requests so retries won't produce duplicate continuations. For streaming you reestablish with a resume token in some cases; we include a recommended pattern in the runbook.
[04:12] [04:45] Priya: I'm going to intentionally trigger a transient failure in the sandbox to show retry behavior. I'll drop the connection and show the client-side backoff.
[04:52] Speaker 3: (noise)
[04:55] Priya: Ok, disconnecting... now the client retries with exponential backoff and then falls back to a lower-cost model variant while we restore the primary.
[05:08] Lina: That fallback behavior is exactly what we need for checkout-critical messages. How do you configure fallback policies?
[05:12] Priya: In Console you can set routing policies per route: prefer low-latency variant, then fallback to cheaper variant, or degrade to async response. We also support canaries for rollouts.
[05:24] Tasha: Do you keep KV cache across requests to reduce tokens? We have repetitive user context that we'd like to avoid sending every time.
[05:30] Priya: Yes — we discuss prefix and KV cache strategies. You can store conversation state in the KV cache and reference it server-side; this can cut token usage significantly and reduce latency.
[05:40] Marcus: Any limits on cache size or eviction?
[05:44] Priya: There are configurable TTLs and size limits per deployment. For high-volume we recommend a dedicated cache tier. We'll include recommended defaults in the runbook.
[05:56] [06:30] Ethan: Switching to failure modes — common pattern: client sees partial stream then connection resets. Recommended flow: client retries with idempotency key, if still failing escalate to fallback model and queue a background refresh.
[06:45] Lina: For PoC we want to simulate 1–5% network packet loss and see user-facing impact. Can Redwood help with that injection in sandbox?
[06:53] Priya: We can provide a synthetic traffic harness and we have a chaos testing config for the sandbox. I can package a script.
[07:02] Tasha: Good. On security — we need SAML SSO and audit logs. Also concerned about token retention and data residency.
[07:08] Ethan: For hosted we provide audit logs, role-based access controls and optional org-level retention. We have region options for data residency in EU/NA. For KMS, we integrate with customer-managed keys for encryption at rest.
[07:24] Marcus: And can we bring-your-own-key (BYOK) for model artifacts?
[07:28] Priya: For Private deployments yes; for hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer KMS keys for customer data. We'll send the exact architecture diagram.
[07:36] [07:58] Priya: Back to parameter tuning — token budgeting example: if average user request is 30 input tokens and target output 40 tokens, set max_tokens to 60 to allow room, and use stop sequences to avoid runaway generation. Also use response truncation fallback for very long prompts.
[08:15] Lina: Do you support streaming partial metadata fields so we can render quick replies separately from the full message?
[08:20] Priya: Yes — we can stream structured output with event types: "partial_text", "final_text", "delta_meta". Console shows structured outputs too.
[08:32] [08:45] Ethan: Question from pricing perspective — are we charged per token even for partial streaming chunks?
[08:50] Priya: Billing is per token generated; partial stream chunks are not double-charged. We also show token usage per call in the Console for visibility.
[09:00] Tasha: For retry cost inflation, what's best practice to bound spend?
[09:04] Priya: Use idempotency and cap retry attempts; use small exponential backoff windows and track retry counts in logs. Also set per-request max_tokens to avoid runaway when retrying with different parameters.
[09:20] [09:40] Priya: Now I'll run a short latency benchmark against hosted in the us-west-2 region — 1k small requests, single token responses, then a 1k mid-sized responses run.
[09:49] Priya: (running) first run looks like P50 72ms, P95 290ms. For mid-sized 40 tokens, P50 140ms, P95 410ms. Caveat: these are sandbox numbers — production routing may vary.
[10:10] Marcus: Those are promising. For our SLA we might need consistent P95 < 300ms — would you recommend Dedicated?
[10:16] Priya: For strict tail SLOs, Dedicated pools or region pinning help. We can run a focused benchmark on Dedicated nodes if you want to see head-to-head numbers.
[10:26] [10:40] Lina: About integrations — we use an internal event bus and prefer webhooks. Is Redwood able to push streaming deltas via websocket to our bus?
[10:48] Ethan: Yes — we support webhooks, websockets, SSE. Many customers forward streaming deltas into their event pipelines.
[10:55] Tasha: One more thing — Do you provide developer SDKs? Our frontend team is React.
[11:00] Priya: We have JS SDK with a streaming client and React examples. We'll include snippets in the quickstart.
[11:08] [11:40] Priya: I'm going to show retry code sample: simple exponential backoff pseudocode, use idempotency-key header, and a resume token for long-running streams.
[11:54] Speaker 4: (agreement)
[11:58] Priya: Note — resume tokens are only supported for sessions under 5min in the hosted tier; for longer sessions we recommend checkpointing conversation state externally.
[12:10] Marcus: That nuance is important. We have multi-minute sessions sometimes.
[12:15] Priya: Then checkpointing on your side or using Dedicated with extended session support is the path. We'll document that.
[12:25] [12:50] Ethan: Let's talk PoC scope. Lina, what's the priority flow you want to test?
[12:56] Lina: Two flows: 1) customer support chat short replies 20–60 tokens; 2) checkout assistant that must be highly reliable and ordered. We'll run a small A/B between your hosted and our in-house endpoint.
[13:10] Tasha: Timeline — we'd like a one-week PoC starting next Monday if possible.
[13:15] Ethan: We can do that. I'll share sandbox access and Priya will run the benchmark script with you.
[13:22] [13:45] Priya: For A/B keep identical prompts and attach idempotency keys so results are comparable. Also ensure clock sync across the clients to measure latencies accurately.
[13:55] Marcus: For telemetry we want per-message tracing. Can Redwood inject trace IDs?
[13:59] Priya: Yes — pass an x-request-id and we will mirror it in logs; Console traces will show the x-request-id.
[14:08] Lina: About compliance docs — do you have an SOC 2 report and pen test summary?
[14:12] Ethan: Yes, I'll send the SOC 2 Type II and our pen test summary; we also have ISO notes.
[14:20] [14:45] Priya: Quick aside — caching again: if you have repeated system prompts, consider using a server-side prefix cache so you don't pay for those tokens every request. There's also an SDK helper to stitch prefixes at the runtime.
[14:58] Tasha: That would help our cost forecasting.
[15:05] Marcus: What about rate-limits for embeddings? We might do embeddings for search in parallel flows.
[15:10] Priya: Embeddings are a separate quota and have a different billing unit. If you run both generative and embedding workloads, Optimize can recommend a split to keep costs down.
[15:22] [15:50] Priya: Now I'll show the Console's Optimize tab — it surfaces model/quantization suggestions, batching settings, and cache recommendations.
[16:02] Priya: For example we recommended q4_0 quantized variant for chat to cut GPU memory while preserving quality; for latency-sensitive flows use fp16 on Dedicated.
[16:18] Lina: Are those suggestions automatically applied?
[16:21] Priya: They are suggestions — you can run an automated experiment or apply them manually. We also do quality regression tests tied to prompt sets to validate.
[16:34] [16:55] Ethan: Ok recapping next steps: Ethan sends sandbox + SOC2; Priya sends benchmark scripts and a short runbook; Lina confirms VPN window; schedule PoC kickoff next Monday. Anyone object?
[17:05] Marcus: No objections.
[17:08] Tasha: Sounds good.
[17:12] [17:30] Priya: Minor note — transcription may show "KV cache" as "V K cache" in some auto transcriptions, so docs will be clearer.
[17:38] Ethan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[17:45] Lina: Appreciate it, talk soon.
[17:48] Marcus: Thanks.
[17:50] Tasha: Bye.

End of transcript.
